T3 Factory / Connected workspaces

One overview.
Independent environments.

Bring two ordinary T3 Code servers into a shared Factory view, organize their projects, and inspect real source-owned files without moving the workspaces into Factory.

Begin the walkthrough →Understand the architectureWhat was demonstrated
Two passive sourcesOne opt-in Factory19 real PNG capturesNo provider turns run
A branch guide, not a release acceptance report.

Factory and T3 Code now build from one repository: the UI lives in apps/factory and is bundled with the server. These real Chrome screenshots were captured before the monorepo migration, including one mobile-width browser view—not a native mobile test. The six thread histories and statuses are explicitly seeded demonstration examples, not evidence of agent execution. Split-mode and fullscreen embedded chat are demonstrated with seeded messages; no agent was started.

01 / Architecture

Factory connects. Sources own the work.

An environment is a running T3 server plus its local state, filesystem, and provider credentials. Factory is another server role—not a migration of those environments into a central workspace.

SOURCE AUTHORITY

Work stays local

Each source owns its project records, threads, files, Git operations, provider subprocesses, and native terminals. Source Alpha and Source Beta have independent profiles.

FACTORY AUTHORITY

Coordination stays shared

Factory persists registrations, groups, and favorites as metadata. Remote projections and subscription cursors are held in memory; protected source credentials belong on the Factory host.

CLIENT ROLE

Presentation stays flexible

Ordinary web, desktop, iOS, and Android clients are presentation layers over a server. This guide demonstrates Chrome, including a mobile-width browser navigator; it does not establish native mobile compatibility or testing.

The hierarchy to keep in mind

A registration identifies a source connection; its environment owns projects, and each project owns durable threads. A thread contains turns. Factory groups organize projects across sources without changing their ownership. A relayed action must retain the exact registration, source environment, and thread target—not just a matching title.

02 / Checkout & isolation

Prepare once. Keep the homes separate.

These commands use one T3 Code checkout, not a global t3 installation. Select Node 24, install dependencies once, and run the combined build below. The server commands then use the built CLI.

SERVER CHECKOUT

~/projects/t3code

feat/t3-serve-factory
Capture baseline: efe7fd7

FACTORY WORKSPACE

apps/factory

Inside the same T3 Code checkout
Shared contracts and one build graph

Every terminal · select runtime, local tools, and clean environment 
cd ~/projects/t3code
nvm use 24.14.0
export PATH="$PWD/node_modules/.bin:$PATH"
unset VITE_DEV_SERVER_URL T3CODE_DEV_AUTH_TOKEN T3CODE_FACTORY_ENABLED

Run this entire setup block in each of all four terminals, including the control shell. Runtime selection, local PATH, and environment cleanup do not carry between terminals. Unsetting the three variables prevents ambient dev-origin, dev-auth, or Factory-role configuration from affecting this isolated demonstration. vp is not installed globally here: the local PATH above makes it available, or use pnpm exec vp when invoking it.

One build for the server and both browser surfaces

Install from the repository root, then build the server and its native web and Factory dependencies together. The server packages both UIs and discovers its bundled Factory assets automatically.

Control shell · install and combined build 
vp i
T3CODE_SINGLE_ORIGIN_DEV=1 vp run build:factory
Never bake in a browser origin.

Do not set VITE_HTTP_URL or VITE_WS_URL. These builds must resolve their backend through the origin serving them, not a hardcoded localhost endpoint.

Choose two real Git workspaces

Use existing Git workspaces, or create the tiny demonstration directories below. These fixtures are a walkthrough convenience, not a requirement for ordinary T3 Code setup.

Control shell · optional demonstration workspaces 
mkdir -p "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-web" \
  "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-api"
git -C "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-web" init -b main
git -C "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-api" init -b main
All paths below are relative to the t3code checkout
Role Isolated home Workspace
Source Alpha .t3/factory-guide/source-alpha .t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-web
Source Beta .t3/factory-guide/source-beta .t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-api
Factory .t3/factory-guide/factory No remote workspace ownership

Each home has its own userdata/statev2.sqlite. Never start this demonstration against, write to, or clean up the live ~/.t3/userdata directory. The commands use --base-dir, the CLI home selector; --home-dir belongs to the dev-runner path and is not substituted here.

03 / Four terminals

Two source servers. One Factory. One control shell.

Keep three foreground server commands running in separate terminals. Use a fourth shell for project registration and one-time source enrollment. Before launching anything, run the full setup block in step 02 independently in all four: checkout directory, Node 24.14.0, local PATH, and the three-variable unset. Each source command below additionally forces T3CODE_FACTORY_ENABLED=false; only the Factory command opts in with --factory.

Terminal 1 · Source Alpha / Atlas Web 
T3CODE_FACTORY_ENABLED=false node apps/server/dist/bin.mjs serve \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3773 \
  --base-dir "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/source-alpha" \
  "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-web"
Terminal 2 · Source Beta / Atlas API 
T3CODE_FACTORY_ENABLED=false node apps/server/dist/bin.mjs serve \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3774 \
  --base-dir "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/source-beta" \
  "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-api"
Terminal 3 · Factory / hosted UI 
node apps/server/dist/bin.mjs serve \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3780 \
  --base-dir "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/factory" \
  --factory --factory-credential-store file

The default serve port is 3773. Ports 3774 and 3780 are explicit choices for this demonstration. Only the third server opts into Factory. The two ordinary sources remain passive.

File credentials are an explicit development choice.

--factory-credential-store file selects a protected-file credential store on the Factory host. The browser cannot enable it and does not retain source bearer credentials in browser storage. Do not treat this flag as a blanket production deployment recommendation.

Optional: give the source projects readable titles

These project commands were executed while the corresponding source servers were running. They operate on the source homes, not Factory's home.

Terminal 4 · control shell / Source Alpha project 
node apps/server/dist/bin.mjs project add \
  --base-dir "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/source-alpha" \
  --title "Atlas Web" \
  "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-web"
Terminal 4 · control shell / Source Beta project 
node apps/server/dist/bin.mjs project add \
  --base-dir "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/source-beta" \
  --title "Atlas API" \
  "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/workspaces/atlas-api"

The running demonstration serves Source Alpha at http://127.0.0.1:3773, Source Beta at http://127.0.0.1:3774, and Factory at http://127.0.0.1:3780/factory/. Loopback examples work only when all three servers are on the same machine.

04 / Browser authorization

Pair with Factory—not with a source.

The browser needs a Factory session with Factory read, control, and administrative scopes. A source enrollment credential is a different authorization step.

  1. Find Factory's fresh startup administrative pairing link.

    Use the private console output in Terminal 3. The full link is intentionally absent from this guide; never publish it or capture its token.

  2. Open that link in the browser you will use for Factory.

    The startup link establishes the browser cookie with Factory scopes. The unauthenticated Factory view links to /pair; an empty token form alone does not authorize the session.

  3. Visit http://127.0.0.1:3780/factory/.

    A newly authenticated Factory starts with an empty overview. You will enroll the two sources next.

Known scope limitation in this branch

Ordinary pair --base-dir against the Factory home currently issues standard native scopes; it does not grant Factory read/control/admin access. If the browser is already paired without those scopes, use a fresh Factory startup administrative link. Do not use the source-enrollment commands below to repair browser authorization.

A cookie for the same localhost hostname can also cover a Vite port, but this walkthrough uses the built, Factory-hosted UI at port 3780. Keep the hostname consistent; localhost and 127.0.0.1 are not interchangeable cookie hosts.

05 / Source authorization

Enroll each source with its own one-time token.

Knowing a host and port is not enough. Enrollment requires both an authorized Factory session and a credential issued by the source being registered.

Terminal 4 · issue a Source Alpha enrollment token 
node apps/server/dist/bin.mjs pair \
  --base-dir "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/source-alpha" \
  --label "T3 Factory"
  1. Go to Serve Nodes → Register source in Factory.

    Enter Source Alpha, scheme HTTP, host 127.0.0.1, and port 3773.

  2. Copy the token from Source Alpha's printed pair URL.

    Paste only the token into the one-time source credential field. Do not open the source pairing link before Factory consumes the token: doing so can use it up.

  3. Register, then repeat with a new token from Source Beta.

    Source tokens expire after five minutes and work once. Issue them just before registration. Never reuse Alpha's token for Beta.

Terminal 4 · issue a distinct Source Beta enrollment token 
node apps/server/dist/bin.mjs pair \
  --base-dir "$PWD/.t3/factory-guide/source-beta" \
  --label "T3 Factory"
Registration values for this same-machine demonstration
Name Scheme / host / port Token issued by
Source Alpha HTTP · 127.0.0.1 · 3773 source-alpha home
Source Beta HTTP · 127.0.0.1 · 3774 source-beta home
Do not enroll Factory itself.

Port 3780 is the Factory endpoint, not a third source. Self-enrollment is forbidden. For a remote source, use an address reachable from the Factory host, not merely from your browser. These loopback values do not describe a cross-machine deployment.

06 / Projects & threads

See the work without flattening its identity.

Expand the source projects to see their thread titles and source identities. Factory brings these projections together; the durable conversations remain in their original source environments.

Demonstration histories—not actual provider runs.

Six threads were created in the native app. Schema-valid historical projection examples were seeded with the servers stopped. The finished, failed, settled, and idle states below illustrate navigation and filtering; no paid provider turns produced them. Fresh source connectivity is real and separate from those seeded work states.

Captures 13 and 14 show the explicitly labeled demonstration messages rendered in native split-mode and fullscreen chat. The setup commands create the topology, not these example histories or the sample orders file; your own content will differ.

Seeded historical thread states in the overview captures
Source / project Thread Demonstration state
Alpha · Atlas Web Order totals and sorting Finished
Alpha · Atlas Web Investigate inventory retry Failed
Alpha · Atlas Web Review shipping permissions Idle
Beta · Atlas API API health endpoint Settled
Beta · Atlas API Review API rollout Finished
Beta · Atlas API Implement inventory pagination Idle

Read two separate signals: work state describes the projected thread history, while freshness describes Factory's current view of that source. A “Finished” historical row is not permission to act on a stale source.

07 / Shared organization

Group the projects. Pin your entry points.

Groups and favorites are shared Factory metadata. Browser-local presentation choices are not shared coordination state.

  1. Create an “Atlas Product” group.

    Use New group and select both Atlas Web and Atlas API. The dialog capture below records both selections.

  2. Pin the group and Atlas Web.

    The favorites and group overview were created through the actual UI, not injected metadata.

  3. Read the tree as displayed.

    In the current tree, pinned Atlas Web appears as a standalone row; the Atlas Product group row displays Beta. That rendering is not evidence that the group was created with only one selected project.

A mobile-width browser navigator

The 430 × 932 capture below shows the real Factory navigator after closing the detail pane. It is a mobile-width browser view, not an iOS or Android native-client test. Truncated labels and horizontally constrained filters are part of this actual captured layout.

Filters are lenses, not disjoint buckets

Available states are All, Active, Waiting, Failed, Settled, Finished, Cancelled, Idle, and Unknown. In these examples, Settled includes completed work, including Finished. Counts overlap; they do not sum to All.

6All
1Failed
3Settled
2Finished
2Idle

Groups and favorites live on the Factory server. Local presentation state lives in the browser. Archive behavior is deferred; this walkthrough does not present an archive/unarchive flow.

08 / Source-owned inspection

Read actual files. Compare the actual working tree.

Choose “Order totals and sorting” from Source Alpha, then inspect Files and Diffs. Factory relays the request to that source's workspace, not to a copied directory on the Factory host.

FILES

The source filesystem

The captured src/orders.ts is a real file in the Atlas Web Git workspace. Its contents are read through the source connection.

DIFFS → WORKING TREE

Unstaged Git changes

The captured diff compares HEAD to the current worktree. Real edits add createdAt, average order value, and newest-first sorting.

Rollback is not workspace restoration in Factory.

Factory rollback changes conversation state with restoreFiles: false. It does not restore workspace files. Do not use a conversation rollback as a substitute for a deliberate source-side Git or file restore.

09 / Runtime model

A turn belongs to the source runtime.

Provider adapters normalize actual provider events. The source server owns Git, file access, provider subprocesses, and PTYs; clients present the state and relay authorized choices.

PROVIDER BOUNDARY

One normalized view

Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, and Antigravity have provider adapters. Normalized events make a shared thread view possible; the graphic is not a promise that every provider supports every action.

CONNECTION BOUNDARY

Freshness before control

Factory uses remote projections and subscription cursors, with reconnect synchronization. A stale or offline source pauses native actions; a cached history is not proof of current authority or completion.

Terminal output has a narrower contract

Factory can attach output only to an existing native PTY, with Factory control authorization and the source's terminal permission. This is not a terminal creation or management interface: it does not create, restart, resize, or send input to a PTY. No terminal demonstration was run here.

10 / Embedded native surface

Native chat, with the source target preserved.

The verified split-mode and fullscreen paths keep browser data requests on Factory while relaying native chat to Source Alpha's selected environment and “Order totals and sorting” thread.

Split-mode and fullscreen ready states demonstrated—not a provider run.

Primary verification held each view ready for at least 60 seconds with native protocol traffic. Seeded demonstration user/assistant messages and the message editor rendered in both views. Browser RPC and HTTP data targets remained on Factory at port 3780.

The check included the persisted composer-context strip setting. The embedded full view did not mount the unsupported workspace-details panel or request unsupported ancillary globals. No new agent turn was started.

Provider eligibility still applies.

A rendered composer is not proof that its installed provider is supported. Arrange the required provider update and authentication on the source before a real new turn. Do not send a paid turn just to reproduce this screenshot.

  1. Choose a fresh source thread from the Factory navigator.

    Confirm both the source label and thread identity; matching titles alone are insufficient.

  2. Open the Chat surface for that selection.

    Both verified views keep browser data requests on Factory, which relays the native surface to the exact registration, source environment, and thread.

  3. For fullscreen, use Expand, then select Chat again.

    Expanding resets the detail surface to Overview. Re-select Chat in the expanded view to load the native conversation; the fullscreen capture below records that actual path.

  4. Verify the ready state before using it.

    Check that the selected conversation, history, and composer correspond to the target. Do not treat a connecting view as a successful attachment, and do not send a paid demonstration turn merely to populate a screenshot.

The single-origin native build from step 02 is necessary for this relay path. The build alone does not establish readiness; captures 13/14 and the primary protocol observations establish split-mode and fullscreen attachment with seeded transcript rendering. Follow-up agent execution is not demonstrated. The native surface separately loads its existing public Google fonts; this portable guide itself has no external assets or requests.

11 / Boundaries & recovery

Control deliberately. Treat stale state honestly.

The walkthrough ends at connected inspection and organization. Starting a provider session is a separate, potentially paid action with prerequisites on the source.

NEW SESSION

Prerequisites before a prompt

A fresh source, an eligible installed and authenticated provider, a title, and a nonempty prompt are required. Check the branch's provider minimum versions before use; outdated installed providers can block native actions.

DEMONSTRATION LIMIT

No hidden provider work

No global provider updates or paid agent turns were performed. Seeded histories do not satisfy provider prerequisites and do not prove successful session creation.

Operational checks and boundaries; disable/re-enable recovery is demonstrated below
Situation What to check or do
Browser paired, Factory access missing Use a fresh Factory startup administrative link. Ordinary pairing against the Factory home supplies native scopes, not Factory read/control/admin scopes.
Source token expired or consumed Issue a fresh token from the matching source home. Do not open its pair URL before Factory enrollment.
Source stale or offline Pause actions. Check the running source and Factory-to-source reachability; retry the connection or use the source-credential re-enrollment workflow when needed. Do not label cached work as newly completed.
Host or port must change The endpoint is immutable. Delete and recreate the registration with the correct endpoint and a fresh source token; this guide does not claim that recovery sequence was tested.
Provider is installed but unsupported Check version eligibility and authentication on the source. Arrange any provider update separately; do not update global tools just to make this demonstration run.
Need files restored Use an intentional source-side file/Git workflow. Factory conversation rollback uses restoreFiles: false.

Disable a registration, then enable it again

This reversible connection recovery was actually tested in the user-owned isolated demonstration. Source Beta's ordinary server kept running passively throughout; disabling its Factory registration is not stopping the source server or interrupting its agents.

  1. Serve Nodes → Manage Source Beta → Disable Source.

    The header changes to 1/2 online. Beta is offline with coverage Not available and zero projected projects/threads; Alpha stays fresh. The notice explicitly says “Agents on the source are not stopped.” Zero projected counts here do not mean the source's projects or histories were deleted.

  2. Manage Source Beta → Enable Source.

    Factory reconnects to the still-running source. The observed result is 2/2 online, both sources fresh, and Beta's one project and three threads visible again. No source-server restart or token re-enrollment was needed.

Shut down only what you started

When finished, stop each foreground server in its own terminal with Ctrl+C. Do not kill by process-name or path patterns, and do not touch other running environments. The isolated homes and workspaces remain on disk for a later walkthrough; this guide includes no destructive cleanup command.

12 / Provenance

What these pictures establish—and what they do not.

All 19 screenshots are actual Chrome captures, including one 430 × 932 mobile-width browser view from the isolated local demonstration. They are embedded PNGs, not reconstructed UI illustrations. The architecture and lifecycle drawings are explanatory graphics, not execution traces.

DEMONSTRATED

Connected inspection and organization

Factory browser pairing; empty authenticated overview; source registration dialog; two connected, fresh sources; native-app-created thread rows; group creation and favorites through the actual UI; a failed-state filter over seeded history; real relayed source files and an actual unstaged working-tree diff; reversible Source Beta disable/re-enable recovery without restarting its server or re-enrolling credentials; split-mode and fullscreen embedded native chat rendering seeded messages and the message editor, each ready for at least 60 seconds with data requests staying on Factory.

NOT DEMONSTRATED

Provider execution and full acceptance

Paid provider turns, real follow-up agent execution, approval/permission execution, archive behavior, checkpoint capture, revert, file restoration, terminal attachment, credential-expiry or re-enrollment recovery, provider interruption/resumption, and native iOS/Android operation. No release-wide or production acceptance claim is made.
